# Signals {#sec-signals}

The comment in the notebook is the right complaint, and it is more precise
than it felt at the time.

R's conditions are S3 objects sitting on a signaling mechanism that can
run a handler while the stack is still alive, muffle a warning, or invoke
a restart. The culture around them is an exception culture: `stop`,
`tryCatch`, unwind, maybe wrap the message in a new class and stop again.
Both facilities are real. One of them is taught. The other is how robust
software actually wants to talk.

## Three moves, not one

Kent Pitman's
[retrospective on condition handling](https://nhplace.com/kent/Papers/Condition-Handling-2001.html)
separates what most languages glue together. The Common Lisp HyperSpec
states the mechanism in
[chapter 9](http://www.lispworks.com/documentation/HyperSpec/Body/09_.htm).
Compressed:

1. **Signal.** Name a situation by allocating an object, not by throwing a
   string.
2. **Handle.** Decide policy while the stack that signaled is still there.
   A handler can repair, muffle, log, or decline.
3. **Restart.** Offer a named way to resume. `invokeRestart` transfers
   control to a restart the signaler, or someone above the signaler,
   established for this purpose.

`tryCatch` does a narrower thing. It establishes an exiting handler. The
stack unwinds to the catch, and then your function runs. Whatever the
callee might have done to fix the problem and continue is gone. That is
the right tool when the policy really is "abandon this attempt." It is
the wrong default when the policy is "hear about this and decide."

`withCallingHandlers` establishes a calling handler. It runs on the live
stack. `withRestarts` and `invokeRestart` are the resume mechanism, and
they are base R, not a package invention. `signalCondition` is the
low-level signal. Warnings and messages are conditions that happen to
have default handlers installed by the runtime: print something, and in
the warning case continue. `tryCatch` on a warning is you replacing that
policy with an unwind. Sometimes you want that. Often you wanted to
muffle, collect, or re-signal.

The R implementation of the split is older than the tidyverse wrappers.
Robert Gentleman and Luke Tierney wrote
[A Prototype of a Condition System for R](https://homepage.stat.uiowa.edu/~luke/R/exceptions/simpcond.html)
and distinguished exiting handlers from calling handlers there. Advanced R's
[conditions chapter](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/conditions.html) is the
practical map, including the class hierarchy (`condition` → `error` /
`warning` / `message`, and your subclasses under those). It also says,
honestly, that restarts are out of its scope. The help pages for
`withRestarts` and `tryCatch` are the reference for the base mechanism.
[rlang::try_fetch()](https://rlang.r-lib.org/reference/try_fetch.html)
is the current "handler that can return a value" spelling, and the `cnd_`
constructors are how you build the objects without hand-rolled `structure()`
calls. None of this is obscure because it is weak. It is obscure because
the first page of search results says `tryCatch`.

## Catching a 500 to throw a 500

The failure mode is a layering mistake.

An HTTP library that sees status 500 has learned a fact. The fact wants a
class: the status, the URL, the body, the request id. That class is the
signal, or it is the value you return if you have chosen errors-as-values
for this boundary. What the application does about it is a different
function, living in a different place.

| Layer | Job |
| --- | --- |
| Library boundary | Signal a classed condition, or return a result value, with enough structure to branch on |
| Policy boundary | `withCallingHandlers` or `try_fetch` map that class onto a recovery, a richer condition, or a logged warning |
| Application boundary | Abort, retry, prompt, or degrade, by invoking a restart or by returning |

Catching an httr2 error solely to `stop()` with a new message throws away
the class the library already gave you and forces every caller to parse
text. Re-signaling a *richer* condition, with the original as the parent,
is a different act: you are translating a transport fact into a domain
fact. The class is the point of the translation. The string is for the
human at the host.

Parent classes matter here. A handler for `http_error` can sit above a
handler for `http_error_500`. A handler for `error` is the wide net.
S3 dispatch on the condition's class is the "native method dispatch" the
comment was reaching for. It works. It works only if someone signals a
class worth dispatching on, and only if the handler is registered where
the stack still has the context to use it.

## Errors as values are a neighboring door

Rust's `Result`, `purrr`'s `safely`, and a validator that returns a
failure value instead of signaling are a different design with the same
taste. The failure is data. The caller branches on it with ordinary
control flow. There is no stack discipline to get right, and there is
also no way for a caller three frames up to establish a restart the
callee can invoke. You chose an explicit return channel over a signal
channel.

R can do both, which means a package has to pick. One effect story per
boundary. Fatal `stop` for programmer errors and invariant failures.
Classed signals for situations a caller might plausibly handle. Result
values when the failure is an ordinary outcome of the domain ("this
address did not geocode") and you do not want it traveling by a side
channel. Mixing all three in one function, plus a `cat()` of the URL for
good measure, is how an API feels schizophrenic.

S7 validators that return character vectors of problems are already in the
errors-as-values family. They are not a condition system. They are a
parse step. Use them at construction. Use conditions for what happens
later, when a well-built value meets a world that can still say no.

## Streams, and the C leak

PowerShell's output streams are the cleanest picture of what a condition
system is *for*, even though the substrate is different. The official list
is in
[about_Output_Streams](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_output_streams):

| Stream | PowerShell | R, if you are disciplined |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Success | pipeline objects | the return value |
| 2 Error | `Write-Error` | an `error` condition |
| 3 Warning | `Write-Warning` | a `warning` |
| 4 Verbose | `Write-Verbose` | a message or a classed condition behind a verbose flag |
| 5 Debug | `Write-Debug` | a debug condition, or cli behind a flag |
| 6 Information | `Write-Information` | a classed message, cli alerts |
| Progress | `Write-Progress`, not redirectable | `cli` progress, or a progress condition |

The win is orthogonal channels. A function can return a value *and* warn
*and* describe what it is doing, and the caller decides what to keep.
PowerShell's redirection (`3>&1`, and the rules in
[about_Redirection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_redirection))
makes that a shell feature. R makes it a handler feature. The idea is the
same: side-channel meaning is structured, and the host picks it up at the
edge.

Two R-specific cuts.

Warnings and messages are already conditions, so they can be muffled,
collected, promoted to errors (`options(warn = 2)` is the blunt version),
or given a class and a handler. `cli` output that goes through the
condition-aware UI is in this world. A hand-rolled `cat()` is not. Text
on the console cannot be dispatched. It can only be captured, and capture
is a miserable API.

C `stdout` and `stderr` are a second console that R's condition system
does not own. A `.Call` that `printf`s has stepped outside the protocol.
Robust packages treat that as a bug unless the foreign chatter is caught
and re-signaled as a condition, or explicitly documented as a debug leak.
The interface principle cuts both ways. You may call C. C does not get to
talk to your user behind the language's back.

## A package doctrine

Small enough to stick on the wall:

- Return values for success. Type them.
- Signal classed conditions for everything a caller might route.
- Prefer calling handlers and `try_fetch` at library boundaries; use
  `tryCatch` when you truly mean "this attempt is over."
- Establish restarts where a caller could plausibly resume: skip this
  record, use this default, retry with this credential.
- Put narration and progress in cli or in messages, behind a preference.
- Do not `cat()` a situation you could signal.
- If C talks, wrap the talk.

This is the functional-core idea applied to communication. The core
returns a value or signals an object. The shell --- the handler, the
option, the CLI flag, the IDE --- decides what the human sees. The next
chapters are about why R grew a core that will not enforce any of this,
and why that is survivable.
